paper.title_en: BFKL as a matrix: anomalous dimensions and running-coupling
paper.abstract_en: The BFKL equation resums high-energy logarithms in a scattering process. We average over the angle between transverse momenta and replace the squared transverse momentum (virtuality) by $D$ discrete cells. The evolution equation becomes a real symmetric $D \times D$ matrix $H_D$. Its off-diagonal entries describe real gluon emissions that move the scale from one cell to another. Its diagonal is the virtual correction that makes those emissions finite. Powers of the matrix build up ordered emission histories, the inverse matrix propagates the amplitude between scales, and the eigenvalues and eigenvectors give the positions and the strengths of the singularities that control growth with rapidity. A row far from both ends of the matrix reproduces the BFKL eigenvalue. Some regions bring corrections to this for a finite Hamiltonian. These are the missing regions below the first cell and above the last cell, and the cell width. Matching the two scale powers allowed by a row yields the anomalous dimension. The matrix reproduces the leading-logarithmic small-$x$ coefficients. At fixed coupling, every finite matrix has only isolated poles. We show that they become increasingly dense as the logarithmic virtuality range grows, with a condition on their residues needed for the sum to approach the continuous BFKL Regge cut. Multiplying each real emission by a Bessel factor, which sums the leading double logarithms of the scale ratio, provides a test of how the fixed-coupling spectrum and its leading eigenvectors respond when long jumps in scale are suppressed. Finally, we place a running coupling which avoids the Landau pole. The number of positive low-scale states grows linearly with the logarithmic length, with a slope fixed by the kernel. A one-loop coupling with Landau pole, combined with a lower wall, creates an ultraviolet turning point and an Airy decay region.
